questions.prompt: What value does the inner declaration use, and which value remains after the if?

options.text: The inner n is 3; the outer n remains 2.
The inner n is 3; the outer n becomes 3.
Both names refer to the same variable, so both are 3.
The declaration is invalid because n already exists.

questions.explanation: The if initializer declares n in the if statement's scope. Its initializer reads the outer n, while the outer variable remains unchanged.

questions.prompt: What happens when this short declaration is used in the same block?

options.text: It assigns 4 to x.
It fails to compile because no name on the left is new in this block.
It declares a new x that shadows the old one.
It changes x's type to int.

questions.explanation: A short declaration may redeclare a variable only when it was declared earlier in the same block and at least one other non-blank name is new. Here x is the only name and is not new.

questions.prompt: What does continue do in this loop?

code.source: for i := 0; i < len(xs); i++ { if xs[i] == 0 { continue } }

options.text: It exits the loop immediately.
It restarts the program at the loop's first statement without checking the condition.
It skips the rest of the current iteration and proceeds to the next iteration.
It skips the next iteration.

questions.explanation: In a for loop, continue advances control to the post statement (or next condition check), skipping the remaining body of the current iteration.

questions.prompt: Does a matching case in a Go expression switch run the following case automatically?

options.text: Yes, every case falls through by default.
Only when cases contain integer constants.
Only when the matching case has no statements.
No; execution leaves the switch unless fallthrough is used.

questions.explanation: Go switch cases do not fall through by default. The fallthrough statement explicitly continues execution into the next case body.

questions.prompt: What is len(view) after these statements?

options.text: It depends on the capacity of base.

questions.explanation: A slice expression base[:2] has length 2. Its capacity may be larger, but capacity does not change its length.

questions.prompt: What does copy(dst, src) return when dst has length 2 and src has length 4?

options.text: 2, the number of elements actually copied.
4, because all source elements are copied by growing dst.
0, because the lengths differ.
It panics because the lengths differ.

questions.explanation: copy copies up to the smaller slice length and returns the number of elements copied. It does not grow the destination.

questions.prompt: How can code distinguish a missing map key from a present key whose value is zero?

options.text: Compare len(m) with zero.
Use m.has(key).
A map lookup always panics for a missing key.
Use value, ok := m[key] and inspect ok.

questions.explanation: The two-result map lookup returns the element value and a boolean indicating whether the key exists, which distinguishes an absent key from a zero value.

questions.prompt: What happens when code assigns a value to a key in a nil map?

options.text: The map is allocated automatically.
The assignment is ignored.
The assignment panics at run time.
The map becomes non-nil but has length zero.

questions.explanation: A nil map can be read and has length zero, but assigning a key requires an initialized map and panics. Use make or a map literal before writing.

questions.prompt: What does the second call to next return?

code.source:
n := 0
next := func() int { n++; return n }
_ = next()
_ = next()

options.text: The closure cannot modify n.

questions.explanation: The function literal closes over the variable n, not a copied value. Each call increments the same captured variable.

questions.prompt: Which value is printed when this function returns?

options.text: The function's return value is printed instead.
The code does not compile because defer arguments are delayed.

questions.explanation: Arguments to a deferred function call are evaluated when the defer statement executes. fmt.Println therefore receives the current value 1 even though x is later changed.

questions.prompt: Which declaration gives a function both a result value and a possible error?

options.text: func load() throws (Record)
func load() (Record) error
func load() (Record, error)
func load() Record, error

questions.explanation: Go functions can declare multiple result types in parentheses. A common convention is to return the result and an error, with nil error indicating success.

questions.prompt: After these statements, what is a.Name?

options.text: "new"
"old"
An empty string
It is unspecified because structs are reference types.

questions.explanation: Assigning a struct value copies its fields. Updating b.Name does not modify a.Name; a struct value is not implicitly a reference.

questions.prompt: A method has receiver *T and T has no corresponding value-receiver method. Which statement is correct?

options.text: *T has the method in its method set; T does not.
Both T and *T implement any interface requiring that method.
Neither T nor *T can implement an interface.
T implements the interface only when stored in a map.

questions.explanation: A pointer receiver method belongs to the method set of *T. A T value does not implement an interface that requires that method, though an addressable T can often call the method through automatic address-taking.

questions.prompt: What is the value of r != nil in this code?

code.source:
var p *bytes.Buffer
var r io.Reader = p
_ = (r != nil)

options.text: false, because p is nil.
It does not compile because nil pointers cannot be interfaces.
It depends on whether the pointer is later dereferenced.
true, because the interface contains a dynamic type (*bytes.Buffer).

questions.explanation: An interface is nil only when both its dynamic type and dynamic value are absent. Here it contains the type *bytes.Buffer and a nil pointer value, so the interface itself is non-nil.

questions.prompt: What does errors.Is(err, target) support when err wraps target with %w?

options.text: It compares only the error messages as strings.
It checks whether target appears in the wrapped error chain.
It unwraps errors only when target is nil.
It converts err into target's concrete type.

questions.explanation: Wrapping an error with %w preserves the error chain. errors.Is traverses that chain and checks for a matching target, including custom Is behavior.

questions.prompt: When should errors.As be used instead of errors.Is?

options.text: To compare an error chain with a sentinel value only.
To turn any error into a string without allocation.
To find an error assignable to a particular concrete or interface type in an error chain.
To check whether an error is nil.

questions.explanation: errors.As searches the error chain for an error assignable to the target type and stores that value. errors.Is is intended for sentinel or custom target matching.

questions.prompt: Which package-level identifier can be used from another Go package?

options.text: Record
parseRecord
recordSize
private_value

questions.explanation: An identifier is exported when its first Unicode letter is uppercase. Other packages can refer to Record, while the lowercase identifiers are unexported.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of t.Helper() inside a test helper function?

options.text: It runs the test in parallel.
It marks the helper so failure locations report the calling test line.
It resets the test's temporary directory.
It makes the helper available to other packages.

questions.explanation: Testing.T.Helper marks the calling function as a test helper so failure reports point to the caller rather than the helper's internal line.

questions.prompt: What does a receive from a closed, drained channel produce when using two assignment targets?

options.text: A panic and false.
The last sent value and true forever.
The receive blocks forever.
The zero value and false.

questions.explanation: Once a channel is closed and all buffered values are received, a receive completes immediately with the element type's zero value and ok=false.

questions.prompt: In a select statement, what happens if multiple cases can proceed immediately?

options.text: The first case in source order always wins.
All ready cases execute in sequence.
One ready case is chosen pseudo-randomly.
The program blocks until exactly one case becomes ready later.

questions.explanation: When multiple communication cases are ready, select chooses one pseudo-randomly. Programs must not rely on source order for priority.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of sync.Mutex around shared mutable state?

options.text: To copy the protected value for every goroutine.
To make a sequence of accesses mutually exclusive when all accesses follow the same locking protocol.
To make every operation in the program atomic automatically.
To schedule goroutines in a fixed order.

questions.explanation: A mutex coordinates goroutines that share state: code locks before accessing the protected state and unlocks afterward. It does not automatically protect accesses that bypass the mutex.

questions.prompt: What is the idiomatic way to avoid leaking a worker blocked while sending after its caller is done?

options.text: Use a cancellation signal or context in a select with the send.
Replace the channel with a larger buffer of any size.
Call runtime.Gosched in the worker.
Close the channel from the receiver while the worker may still send.

questions.explanation: A worker can select between sending and cancellation, allowing it to stop when the caller no longer needs the result. A buffer only postpones blocking and closing while sends remain possible can panic.

questions.prompt: Which statements about Go variable declarations and scope are correct?

options.text: A declared local variable receives its type's zero value when no initializer is given.
A short declaration can introduce a package-level variable.
A short declaration may reuse a same-block variable if another non-blank name is new.
A name declared in an inner block is visible after that block ends.

questions.explanation: Local variables without explicit initializers receive zero values. Short declarations are permitted in function bodies and nested blocks, and same-block redeclaration requires at least one new non-blank variable.

questions.prompt: Which statements about loops and control flow are correct?

options.text: continue is valid to continue an enclosing switch statement.
A for loop is Go's loop construct and can omit its init or post clause.
A labeled break can exit the labeled loop from inside nested control flow.
break exits the innermost enclosing for, switch, or select unless labeled.

questions.explanation: Go uses for for loop forms with optional clauses. Unlabeled break exits the innermost loop, switch, or select; labeled break can target an enclosing statement. continue applies to loops, not switches.

questions.prompt: Which statements about slices are correct?

options.text: A slice value describes a segment of an underlying array.
Appending may allocate a new underlying array when capacity is insufficient.
Assigning one slice to another always copies every element into independent storage.
A two-index slice expression may have length greater than capacity.

questions.explanation: Slices refer to an underlying array through a pointer, length, and capacity. Append can reuse or replace that array depending on capacity. Slice assignment copies only the slice descriptor, and length cannot exceed capacity.

questions.prompt: Which statements about Go maps are correct?

options.text: A map lookup for a missing key returns the element type's zero value.
Map iteration order is guaranteed to be insertion order.
A nil map can be ranged over safely.
Concurrent reads and writes to the same ordinary map require synchronization.

questions.explanation: A missing key yields the zero value; a nil map can be read and ranged over. Map iteration order is unspecified, and unsynchronized concurrent read/write access is not safe.

questions.prompt: Which statements about closures are correct?

options.text: A closure always receives an independent snapshot of every captured variable.
A closure can refer to variables from its enclosing function.
Calling a closure can observe changes to a captured variable.
A function literal cannot be assigned to a variable.

questions.explanation: Function literals can be assigned and may close over variables in their surrounding scope. Closures refer to captured variables, so later mutations may be observed when the closure runs.

questions.prompt: Which statements about defer are correct?

options.text: Deferred calls run when the surrounding function returns, including during panic unwinding.
Multiple deferred calls run in last-in, first-out order.
A defer inside a loop runs at the end of each loop iteration.
Arguments to a deferred call are generally evaluated when defer executes.

questions.explanation: Deferred calls run as the function returns or unwinds from panic and are executed in LIFO order. Call arguments are evaluated at the defer statement; a defer in a loop remains pending until the surrounding function returns.

questions.prompt: Which statements about structs and methods are correct?

options.text: A struct assignment copies the struct's field values.
A struct's unexported fields become accessible to every importing package.
Embedding a type automatically makes every method promoted to every value of that type.
A pointer receiver can modify the pointed-to struct when called on an addressable value.

questions.explanation: Struct assignment copies fields (though copied fields such as pointers can still refer to shared data). Pointer receiver methods can mutate their receiver. Unexported fields remain package-scoped, and method promotion depends on the embedding form and method set.

questions.prompt: Which statements about interface satisfaction are correct?

options.text: A nil pointer stored in an interface makes the interface itself nil.
A type satisfies an interface implicitly by implementing its required methods.
An interface value can hold a concrete value and its dynamic type.
An interface can be assigned only when a type explicitly declares implements.

questions.explanation: Go uses implicit interface satisfaction based on method sets. Interface values carry a dynamic type and value; a typed nil pointer makes the interface non-nil, and no implements declaration is required.

questions.prompt: Which statements about error handling are sound?

options.text: Callers should check an error result before using a result that is invalid on failure.
Wrapping with %w can preserve an error for errors.Is or errors.As.
Returning a useful error can add context with fmt.Errorf and %w.
Comparing error strings is the preferred replacement for errors.Is.

questions.explanation: Go code handles errors as returned values. Check them according to the function contract, and use %w when adding context while preserving the wrapped error chain; string matching is brittle.

questions.prompt: Which statements about packages are correct?

options.text: Files in the same directory normally belong to the same package name.
An imported package's lowercase identifiers are accessible to importers.
An identifier beginning with an uppercase letter is exported from its package.
Import aliases can provide a local name for an imported package.

questions.explanation: A directory's Go source files are organized into a package, exported identifiers begin with uppercase letters, and import aliases change the local package name. Lowercase identifiers remain unexported.

questions.prompt: Which practices fit Go's testing package?

options.text: Put ordinary package tests in files ending with _test.go.
Name a test function TestXxx and accept *testing.T.
A test function must return bool to signal success.
Call t.Fatal when a test must stop after a failed prerequisite.

questions.explanation: Go tests are discovered in _test.go files. Test functions use the Test prefix and *testing.T parameter; Fatal records a failure and stops that test goroutine. Tests do not return bool.

questions.prompt: Which statements about channels are correct?

options.text: A send on an unbuffered channel waits for a corresponding receive to rendezvous.
Closing a channel prevents future sends and makes receives eventually complete.
Sending on a closed channel panics.
The receiver is generally responsible for closing a channel after all sends.

questions.explanation: An unbuffered send synchronizes with a receive. Closing indicates no more values will be sent; receives drain buffered values and then return zero values. Sending after close panics, so the sender that knows no more sends will occur normally closes it.

questions.prompt: Which statements about goroutines and shared state are correct?

options.text: Starting a goroutine guarantees it finishes before its caller returns.
Unsynchronized concurrent writes to the same variable are safe if each writes an integer.
A mutex can protect shared mutable state when every relevant access uses it.
A channel send and corresponding receive can synchronize goroutines.

questions.explanation: Goroutines execute independently and are not implicitly joined to their caller. Mutexes and channel communication provide synchronization when used consistently; conflicting unsynchronized accesses constitute a data race.

questions.prompt: Which statements about select are correct?

options.text: When several cases are ready, source order defines a guaranteed priority.
A select with no cases blocks forever.
A default case runs immediately when no communication case is ready.
A nil channel case can never proceed.

questions.explanation: With no ready communication, default is selected if present; without cases, select blocks forever. A nil channel is never ready. If multiple cases are ready, selection is pseudo-random rather than source-ordered.

questions.prompt: Which statements describe common Go edge cases correctly?

options.text: Appending to a nil slice is valid and returns a usable slice.
Taking the address of a map element is permitted.
A zero-value sync.Mutex is ready for use.
A receive-only channel can be used to send values.

questions.explanation: Appending allocates storage when needed, including from a nil slice. Map elements are not addressable, a zero-value Mutex is usable, and a receive-only channel cannot send.

questions.prompt: Match each expression to its result or behavior.

rows.label: Receive from closed and drained channel

columns.label: Element zero value; ok=false in comma-ok form
Valid; returns a slice with the value

questions.explanation: Missing map reads return the element zero value; a nil-map assignment panics. A drained closed-channel receive returns zero and false, while append works on a nil slice.

questions.prompt: Match each declaration to its scope or visibility.

rows.label: Name declared in an if initializer

columns.label: Visible in the if statement's scope
Not valid in this declaration context

questions.explanation: An if initializer's declaration is scoped to the if statement. Short declarations are function-body syntax; identifier capitalization controls export visibility.

questions.prompt: Match each control statement to its effect.

rows.label: Unlabeled break in nested control flow

columns.label: Exits the innermost loop, switch, or select
Continues into the next case body

questions.explanation: continue advances a loop; break exits the innermost eligible construct; fallthrough explicitly enters the next switch case; return leaves the function.

questions.prompt: Match each Go test or package convention to its purpose.
questions.explanation: Go's testing tool discovers tests in _test.go files, recognizes Test functions with *testing.T, and t.Helper improves failure locations. Uppercase identifiers are exported.

questions.prompt: Match each concurrency operation to its synchronization or state behavior.

columns.label: Allows another lock operation to proceed
One ready case is chosen without source-order priority

questions.explanation: Unbuffered communication rendezvous with a receiver. Unlock releases a mutex; nil channel operations are never ready, and select does not prioritize ready cases by source order.
